DOCUMENT:
Pricing Proposal: Introducing an Off-Peak Membership
Pulse Fitness, Commercial Team, August 2026

1. Proposal
We propose introducing an off-peak membership at £29 a month from 1 October 2026, alongside our existing standard membership at £42 a month. Off-peak members would have access before 4 pm on weekdays and all day at weekends, with full access to the gym floor and to classes running in those hours.

2. Background
Pulse operates four clubs with 9,600 standard members. Membership has been flat for 18 months, while two budget gyms have opened within our catchments, both offering memberships at £22 to £25 a month. Our clubs are busy between 5 pm and 8 pm on weekdays, when the gym floor often runs at or near capacity, but quiet during weekday daytimes, when typical utilisation is around 30%.

Access-control data for May to July 2026 show that 31% of our current standard members visit exclusively in what would be the off-peak window, and a further 22% visit mostly off-peak.

3. Market evidence
A survey of 640 non-members living within two miles of our clubs, conducted in June, found that 19% would "definitely" or "probably" join at £29 a month for off-peak access. The most interested groups were retirees, shift workers, parents of school-age children and students.

Four of our six closest competitors already offer an off-peak or daytime membership, priced between £25 and £32.

4. Classes and retention
Retention is the other half of our commercial challenge. Monthly churn among members who attend at least one class a week is 2.1%, against 4.8% among members who do not attend classes. Classes clearly keep members loyal, so we will add six extra daytime classes per club each week to support the new membership, which should lower churn among off-peak members towards the 2.1% level. The additional classes would cost £18,700 a month across the four clubs in instructor fees.

5. Revenue projection
We expect to recruit 1,200 new off-peak members in the first year, about 300 per club, which is consistent with the survey response and the size of our catchments. At £29 a month, this is £34,800 a month, or £417,600 a year, in new membership revenue. After the cost of the additional classes (£224,400 a year), net additional revenue is £193,200 a year.

Because daytime utilisation is low, the additional members can be accommodated without investment in equipment or space.

6. Operational changes
Access control will be updated so that off-peak members' cards do not open the turnstiles outside their access window. Off-peak members will have weekday access until 5 pm, giving those finishing early shifts or school pick-ups time to train. Members will be able to upgrade to standard membership at any time, and to switch between membership types with one month's notice.

7. Risks
Some standard members may perceive the off-peak price as unfair. We will communicate the change as an extension of choice. Competitor responses are possible; the budget gyms already price below our proposed off-peak rate, so we do not expect a price war.

8. Staff consultation
Club managers and front-of-house teams at all four clubs were consulted in July. Managers supported the proposal, noting that daytime classes are often under-filled and that a daytime membership would help build a regular community at quieter times. Front-of-house staff asked for clear signage and app messaging about access hours, which we will provide before launch.

9. Recommendation
The off-peak membership fills spare daytime capacity, responds to competitor offers and targets clearly identified customer groups. We project net additional revenue of around £193,000 a year and recommend launch on 1 October 2026.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Off-peak members will have weekday access until 5 pm" -- Section 1 defines off-peak access as before 4 pm on weekdays; section 6 says off-peak members have weekday access until 5 pm (also into the busy 5-8 pm period the document says is near capacity). The access window contradicts itself.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "Classes clearly keep members loyal, so we will add six extra daytime classes per club each week" -- The churn difference is correlational: members who choose to attend classes weekly are likely more engaged/committed to begin with (self-selection). It does not show classes cause lower churn, nor that adding classes would bring off-peak churn to 2.1%.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "At £29 a month, this is £34,800 a month, or £417,600 a year, in new membership revenue." -- The projection counts only new members and ignores downgrades, although the document states 31% of the 9,600 standard members (about 2,976) already visit only off-peak and can switch with one month's notice. If they downgraded, revenue would fall by about £13 x 2,976 = £38,700 a month (about £464,000 a year), more than wiping out the projected gain.

REVIEW:
# Review: Off-Peak Membership Proposal

The proposal is clearly written and the arithmetic in Section 5 checks out. However, it leaves out the largest financial effect of the change. Once that is included, the projected £193,000 gain could become a loss. The overall assessment is in the summary at the end.

## 1. Downgrades by existing members (critical)

Section 2 reports that **31% of current standard members already visit only during the off-peak window**. That is about 2,976 members who could switch from £42 to £29 and lose nothing. Section 6 makes this easy, since members can switch membership types on one month's notice.

The proposal never uses this figure in the projection, and Section 7 treats the issue only as a matter of perceived fairness. The numbers:

| Scenario | Annual revenue lost |
|---|---|
| All 2,976 exclusive off-peak members downgrade (£13 × 12 each) | **£464,256** |
| Downgrades needed to wipe out the £193,200 net gain | ~1,240 members (13% of the base, or 42% of the exclusive off-peak group) |

So if fewer than half of the members who already train only off-peak downgrade, the proposal loses money. The further 22% who visit "mostly" off-peak are extra exposure on top of that.

Your summary says "members who want more can upgrade at any time." The more important movement is the opposite one, and the projection needs to model it directly. Options include:
- an explicit downgrade assumption with sensitivity analysis;
- off-peak for new joiners only, or a minimum tenure before switching;
- a narrower window or different price.

## 2. Inconsistent access window

- Section 1 says access ends **before 4 pm**.
- Section 6 says access runs **until 5 pm**.

This matters. Section 2 says peak begins at 5 pm, so a 5 pm cutoff runs right up to peak and widens the group of current members who could downgrade. It also affects capacity planning. Choose one window and use it throughout.

## 3. First-year revenue is overstated

£417,600 assumes all 1,200 new members pay for all 12 months. In practice:
- **Recruitment is spread over the year.** If sign-ups are roughly even, average tenure in year one is about 6 months.
- **Members churn.** The projection applies no churn at all, even at the 2.1% rate the proposal hopes for.

A realistic year-one figure is closer to £180,000–£210,000 gross. After the £224,400 class cost, that is a small loss before any downgrades. Present year one and run-rate separately.

## 4. The case for extra classes is weak

- **Correlation, not causation.** People who attend classes probably differ from those who don't in commitment, social ties and schedule. Adding classes won't necessarily bring new members' churn down to 2.1%.
- **The benefit isn't counted.** The full £224,400 cost is in the projection, but the retention gain is not. Your summary calls the classes "an investment," but the document never shows the return.
- **Managers say daytime classes are already under-filled** (Section 8). That suggests filling existing classes before adding 24 more a week.
- **Unit cost.** £18,700 a month for about 104 classes works out to roughly £180 per class. Check whether this is right.

## 5. Demand evidence needs support

- The 19% "definitely/probably" figure is stated intent. Actual conversion is usually much lower; a common rule of thumb is to count only a fraction of "definitely" responses and few "probably" ones.
- Your summary says 300 per club is "well within what the survey implies," but the document gives no catchment population, so readers can't check this. Show the calculation: adults in catchment × response rate × conversion discount.
- New members joining to train off-peak is likely, but some survey respondents may be people who would otherwise have joined later at £42.

## 6. Capacity and cost claims

- The 30% utilisation figure covers **weekday daytimes only**. Off-peak access includes **all day at weekends**, and weekend utilisation isn't given.
- "Without investment" may be true for equipment, but variable costs such as cleaning, towels, wear and reception cover are absent from the "net" figure. The result is really revenue minus class costs, not net revenue.
- No marketing or launch costs are included.

## 7. Competitive risk is understated

Budget gyms offer **full access at £22–£25**, below the £29 off-peak price. The price-sensitive groups you are targeting (students, retirees) may find this the more attractive offer. Explain why they would pay more at Pulse for less access.

## Summary

| Issue | Severity |
|---|---|
| Downgrades by existing members not modelled | **Critical**: could reverse the result |
| 4 pm vs 5 pm window inconsistency | High |
| Year-one revenue ignores ramp-up and churn | High |
| Class cost included, retention benefit not; causal claim unsupported | Medium |
| Survey-to-projection link not shown | Medium |
| Weekend capacity, variable costs, marketing omitted | Low–Medium |

The idea itself may still be sound, since competitors offer similar products and daytime capacity exists. But the current document does not support "low-risk" or "around £193,000 a year." A revised version should include a downgrade scenario, a monthly ramp-up model with churn, and a fixed access window before it goes forward.
